means: Active-passive keeps a standby idle and fails over. Active-active serves from both and must resolve conflicting writes.
example: Active-passive is far simpler and wastes the standby's capacity. Active-active doubles usable capacity and forces you to answer 'what if both regions write the same row?'
diagram:
Active-passive: standby idle, promote on failure
  simple, RTO = failover time, capacity wasted

Active-active: both serve
  no failover delay, full capacity,
  conflict resolution is now YOUR problem

means: A translation layer between your model and an external or legacy one, so their concepts don't leak into your domain.
example: A payment provider's 20-field webhook payload is translated into your four-field PaymentResult at the boundary. Switching providers touches one adapter, not forty files.
diagram:
external model → [ ACL adapter ] → your model
                        ↑
        all provider quirks stop here

Without it, the vendor's schema becomes yours forever

means: A strategy for changing an API without breaking existing clients. Mobile apps you cannot force-update make this permanent, not optional.
example: An old app version stays in use for 18 months. Removing a field is a crash for those users, so v1 must keep working while v2 exists alongside it.
diagram:
URL:    /v1/orders, /v2/orders   (explicit, clear)
Header: Accept-Version               (clean URLs)
Field-level: additive only, never remove

Also decide: deprecation window, sunset headers,
             how you'll know who's still on v1

means: For work too slow for a request cycle: accept it, return a job ID immediately, and let the client poll or receive a callback.
example: A 4-minute document analysis behind a synchronous endpoint hits every gateway timeout. Returning 202 with a status URL makes the slowness a first-class part of the API.

means: An append-only record of who did what, when, and to which resource. Regulators and incident reviews both need it, and neither accepts 'we have application logs'.
example: 'Who changed this customer's credit limit in March?' is unanswerable from application logs. A dedicated immutable audit table with actor, action, target, before and after answers it.
diagram:
actor + action + target + timestamp
  + before/after + request id + ip

Append-only, separate store, own retention
Never mixed into debug logs (different lifecycle)

means: Availability multiplies across dependencies in series. Adding components lowers your ceiling unless they're redundant.
example: Three services each at 99.9% in a request path give 99.7% combined — 26 hours of downtime a year, not 8.7. Redundancy is what pushes it back up.
diagram:
99.9%   → 8.7 hrs/year
99.99%  → 52 min/year
99.999% → 5 min/year

In series:  0.999³ = 99.7%  (worse)
In parallel: 1-(0.001)² = 99.9999% (better)

means: Rough arithmetic done early to rule architectures in or out before you build anything. Being within an order of magnitude is the whole point.
example: 10M daily users × 20 requests = 200M/day ≈ 2,300 req/sec average. Peak at 3x is ~7,000/sec. That number alone tells you whether one database will do.
diagram:
DAU × actions/day = daily requests
÷ 86,400            = average req/sec
× peak factor (2-5x) = peak req/sec

2,300/s avg → 7,000/s peak
One Postgres? Maybe. One Postgres for writes? No.

means: Populating new columns or systems with historical data without taking production down. Volume makes the naive approach impossible.
example: One UPDATE across 80M rows locks the table and blows up replication lag. Batches of 5,000 with a pause, throttled on replica lag, takes hours and hurts nobody.
diagram:
UPDATE 80M rows → lock, WAL flood, replica lag ✗

loop: 5,000 rows → commit → sleep
      pause if replica lag > 5s
resumable (track last id), idempotent, observable

means: Backward compatible means new code reads old data. Forward compatible means old code tolerates new data — which is what makes rolling deploys safe.
example: During a rolling deploy both versions run at once. If the old version crashes on an unknown enum value, every deploy is a partial outage.
diagram:
Backward: new code reads old data ✓
Forward:  old code ignores unknown fields ✓
   ↓
Safe: add optional fields, add enum values
      that old code can ignore
Unsafe: rename, remove, retype, change semantics

means: A boundary within which a term has one unambiguous meaning. Two contexts can both have a 'Customer' and correctly mean different things.
example: In billing, a Customer has a tax ID and payment terms. In support, a Customer has a ticket history and a sentiment score. Forcing one shared model makes both worse.
diagram:
Billing:  Customer = tax id, terms, invoices
Support:  Customer = tickets, SLA tier, contacts
Shipping: Customer = addresses, delivery prefs

One shared "Customer" table serves none of them well

means: The gap between normal load and your breaking point. Running at 80% of capacity looks efficient and leaves no room to absorb a spike or a failed node.
example: A cluster at 85% CPU cannot survive one node loss — the survivors need 100%. Target 50-60% steady state so failure and traffic spikes are both absorbable.
diagram:
target steady state: 50-60%
  ↓ absorbs: 1 node loss, 2x spike,
             deploy overhead, GC pauses

85% steady state = one bad Tuesday from cascading

means: Choreography means services react to events with no central brain. Orchestration means one coordinator drives the steps. Choreography scales; orchestration is debuggable.
example: A 7-step order flow in pure choreography is impossible to trace when step 5 silently never fires. An orchestrator makes the state machine explicit and queryable.
diagram:
Choreography: A→event→B→event→C
  decoupled, no single owner,
  emergent behaviour nobody can draw

Orchestration: coordinator → A, B, C
  explicit state, easy to trace,
  coordinator becomes a dependency

means: Splitting a large upload into parts so a dropped connection resumes rather than restarts, and no single request holds 2GB.
example: A 2GB upload on mobile fails at 90% and restarts from zero. With 8MB chunks and a resume token, it continues from chunk 231.
diagram:
file → 8MB chunks
  upload each with an index + upload id
  server tracks received chunks
  drop → client asks "what's missing?" → resume ✓
  all received → assemble + verify checksum

means: Coupling is how much modules depend on each other; cohesion is how related the things inside a module are. Good design maximises cohesion and minimises coupling.
example: A 'utils' module is low cohesion — nothing in it belongs together. Two services that must always deploy together are high coupling — they're really one service.
diagram:
High cohesion: everything in the module
               serves one purpose
Low coupling:  changing module A rarely
               forces a change in B

"These two always deploy together" = one service

means: OFFSET makes the database count and discard rows, so deep pages get slower and results shift as data changes. Cursors seek directly to a position.
example: `OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20` scans half a million rows to throw them away. `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) LIMIT 20` uses the index and is constant time.
diagram:
OFFSET 500000 → scan + discard 500k rows ✗
  also: new rows shift pages, items duplicate/vanish

Cursor: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?)
  constant time, stable ✓
  cost: no random page access

means: Modelling a pipeline as a directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies, so independent branches run in parallel and failures retry at task level.
example: A nightly pipeline of 40 sequential steps takes 6 hours. As a DAG, independent branches run in parallel and it finishes in 90 minutes — and a failed task retries alone.
diagram:
┌ extract_a ┐
start ┤             ├ join → transform → load
      └ extract_b ┘

Parallel where possible, retry per task,
backfill a single date range

means: Legal requirements that certain data physically stays in a jurisdiction. It constrains architecture before any technical consideration does.
example: If EU user data cannot leave the EU, a single global primary is illegal regardless of how well it performs. That shapes sharding, backups and even log routing.
diagram:
Constrains: primary location, replicas, backups,
            logs, analytics exports, support tooling

Usually forces regional sharding by user
Check before designing, not during audit

means: Deciding how long each class of data lives and how it's actually removed — including from backups, replicas, caches, logs and the warehouse.
example: Deleting a user row leaves them in nightly backups, the search index, the analytics warehouse and six months of logs. Crypto-shredding solves the backup problem.
diagram:
delete request → primary ✓ replicas ✓ cache ✓
              → search index ✓ warehouse ✓ logs ✓
              → backups ✗ (can't rewrite them)

Crypto-shredding: per-user key, destroy the key
                  → backup ciphertext is unreadable

term: Data Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse
means: A warehouse stores structured, modelled data. A lake stores raw files of any shape. A lakehouse puts warehouse table semantics on top of lake storage.
example: Dumping everything into a lake with no catalog or schema produces a data swamp nobody can query. Table formats like Iceberg or Delta are what prevent that.
diagram:
Lake:      raw files, cheap, schema-on-read
Warehouse: modelled tables, fast, schema-on-write
Lakehouse: lake storage + ACID table format
           (Iceberg / Delta / Hudi)

Lake with no governance = swamp

means: Each service owns its schema and no other service reads it directly. It's the boundary that makes microservices real rather than a distributed monolith.
example: Two services sharing a table means neither can change its schema alone — you've paid the microservice cost and kept the monolith's coupling.
diagram:
Shared DB: service B reads A's tables
  → A cannot change its schema ✗
  → distributed monolith

Own DB: access only via A's API/events ✓
  cost: no joins across services, eventual consistency

means: Collecting individual per-item lookups within one tick and issuing them as a single batched query. The standard fix for GraphQL's N+1 problem.
example: A query resolving 50 posts each fetching an author issues 51 queries. A DataLoader collapses the 50 author lookups into one `WHERE id IN (...)`.
diagram:
resolver calls load(1), load(2), ... load(50)
  ↓ batched within the same tick
one query: WHERE id IN (1..50)
  ↓ results distributed back

51 queries → 2. Also dedupes repeated ids.

means: Deliberately duplicating data to avoid joins on a hot read path. You trade write complexity and consistency risk for read speed.
example: A feed query joining five tables takes 400ms. Storing a precomputed feed row takes 8ms — and now every author name change must fan out to those rows.
diagram:
5-way join → 400ms
precomputed row → 8ms ✓

Cost: writes fan out, data can drift
Rule: denormalise for a MEASURED read problem,
      never pre-emptively

means: Generating unique IDs across many nodes without coordination. Random UUIDv4 destroys index locality; time-ordered IDs preserve it.
example: Switching a high-insert table from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 cut index bloat sharply — inserts append to the right edge of the B-tree instead of scattering across it.
diagram:
UUIDv4:  random → every insert a random B-tree page ✗
UUIDv7 / ULID / Snowflake:
  [ timestamp | node | sequence ]
  → sortable, append-friendly, still unique ✓

Auto-increment: ordered, but needs coordination

means: Encrypting data with a per-object data key, then encrypting that key with a master key held in a KMS. Rotating the master key doesn't require re-encrypting the data.
example: 10TB encrypted with 4M data keys. Rotating the master key re-wraps 4M small keys instead of rewriting 10TB of ciphertext.
diagram:
data → encrypted with data key (DEK)
DEK  → encrypted with master key (KEK, in KMS)
stored: ciphertext + wrapped DEK

Rotate KEK → re-wrap DEKs only, data untouched

means: ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw and transforms inside the warehouse. ELT won because storage got cheap and warehouses got fast.
example: With ELT the raw data is retained, so when the transform logic turns out to be wrong you re-run it. With ETL, the pre-transform data is gone.
diagram:
ETL: extract → transform → load (raw discarded)
ELT: extract → load raw → transform in-warehouse ✓
                  ↑
      bad transform? re-run it. Raw is still there.

means: Moving data to cheaper, slower storage as it ages, because access frequency drops far faster than data volume.
example: Last 30 days on SSD, 30-365 days on object storage, older in archive. Storage cost drops by an order of magnitude and 95% of queries never notice.
diagram:
0-30d    SSD / hot         ← 95% of queries
30-365d  object storage     ← occasional
1y+      archive (glacier)  ← audit only

Define the retrieval SLA per tier BEFORE moving data

means: A map from term to the list of documents containing it. It's what makes full-text search fast, and why search engines are not databases.
example: Finding 'payment failed' across 40M documents by scanning is impossible. An inverted index intersects two posting lists and returns in milliseconds.
diagram:
"payment" → [doc 3, 91, 402, ...]
"failed"  → [doc 91, 402, 8871, ...]
             ↓ intersect
          [91, 402]

Then score by relevance (BM25) and rank

means: Scheduled work needs the same rigour as request handling: what happens on overlap, on missed runs, on partial failure, and when two instances both fire.
example: A cron running on every replica fires six times. One that takes 70 minutes on a 60-minute schedule overlaps itself. Both are silent until they corrupt something.
diagram:
Decide explicitly:
  overlap?   → lock, or skip if still running
  missed?    → catch up, or skip
  duplicate? → leader election / distributed lock
  partial?   → idempotent + resumable
  visible?   → alert on "didn't run", not just "failed"

means: B-trees update in place — good for reads, random writes. LSM trees append to memory then flush sorted files — excellent write throughput, reads may check several files.
example: Postgres uses B-trees; Cassandra, RocksDB and LevelDB use LSM. A write-heavy time-series workload on a B-tree thrashes; on an LSM it's sequential.
diagram:
B-tree: in-place update, random I/O,
        fast reads, slower writes
LSM:    memtable → flush → sorted files
        sequential writes ✓, reads check many files,
        needs compaction

means: Turning an uploaded original into the derivatives you serve — thumbnails, transcodes, previews — asynchronously, because it's slow and CPU-heavy.
example: Generating five thumbnail sizes inline makes upload take 12 seconds. Uploading raw, returning immediately, and processing off a queue makes it feel instant.
diagram:
upload original → S3 → event → queue
  ↓ workers
thumbnails, transcodes, OCR, virus scan
  ↓ write derivative locations
UI shows a placeholder until ready

Keep the original. Derivatives are re-derivable.

means: One deployable with hard internal module boundaries. You get most of the design discipline of microservices without the distributed-systems tax.
example: Modules communicate only through published interfaces, each owns its tables, and no module imports another's internals. Extracting one into a service later is then mechanical.
diagram:
single deploy
 ├ module: billing   (owns billing_* tables)
 ├ module: catalog   (owns catalog_* tables)
 └ module: identity

Cross-module access only via public interface
→ extract to a service when a team needs it

means: Microservices buy independent deployment and scaling, and cost you network failure, distributed transactions and operational overhead. Most teams pay before they need the benefit.
example: Six engineers running eleven services spend more time on service plumbing than on product. The same team on a modular monolith ships faster and can split later.
diagram:
Monolith:      1 deploy, in-process calls, easy txns
Microservices: independent deploys + scaling
               distributed txns, network failure,
               tracing, service discovery, versioning

The split is justified by TEAM boundaries,
not by code size.

means: Running in more than one region for latency or survivability. The hard part is never the compute — it's the data.
example: Stateless services in three regions is a weekend. Deciding what happens to writes when regions can't reach each other is the actual multi-region project.
diagram:
Easy:  stateless compute in N regions
Hard:  where do writes go?
       what's the conflict resolution?
       what's the failover data loss (RPO)?
       what does data residency law require?

means: Whether tenants share infrastructure. Pooled is cheap and risks cross-tenant leakage; siloed is isolated and expensive; bridge splits the difference.
example: Pooled with a tenant_id column costs one missing WHERE clause to leak data. Schema-per-tenant makes leakage structurally harder and complicates migrations across 4,000 schemas.
diagram:
Pool:   shared tables + tenant_id
        cheapest, one bug = leak, noisy neighbours
Bridge: shared cluster, schema/db per tenant
Silo:   separate stack per tenant
        strongest isolation, highest cost

Enterprise tier often BUYS the silo

means: One tenant's load degrading everyone else's experience on shared infrastructure.
example: One customer's bulk import consumes the entire connection pool and every other tenant sees timeouts. Per-tenant quotas and separate queues contain it.
diagram:
tenant A: bulk import ████████████████
tenant B: ▏ starved
tenant C: ▏ starved

Fix: per-tenant rate limits, separate queues,
     fair scheduling, dedicated pools for big accounts

means: Fan-out to email, push, SMS and in-app with per-user preferences, deduplication, batching and quiet hours. Deceptively large.
example: 'Send an email on comment' becomes: don't notify the author of their own comment, batch 30 comments into one digest, respect quiet hours, and never send twice on retry.
diagram:
event → preference check → channel routing
      → dedupe window → batching/digest
      → quiet hours → rate cap per user
      → provider (with fallback) → delivery tracking

The fan-out is easy. The suppression rules are the system.

means: Money needs an append-only, double-entry ledger — never a mutable balance column. The balance is derived, and every change has a traceable cause.
example: `UPDATE balance SET amount = amount - 500` loses all history and races. Two ledger entries that must sum to zero are auditable and reconcilable.
diagram:
Never: UPDATE balance SET amount = amount - 500

Ledger (append-only, immutable):
  entry 1: account A  -500
  entry 2: account B  +500
  ↓ must sum to zero
balance = SUM(entries), or a cached snapshot

means: Counting usage per tenant for both enforcement and billing. It must be accurate enough to invoice and cheap enough to run on every request.
example: Counting in-process gives wrong totals across replicas. Counting synchronously in Postgres adds a write to every request. Redis counters flushed periodically is the usual compromise.
diagram:
per request: INCR in Redis (fast, approximate)
periodically: flush to durable store (billable truth)

Decide: hard limit or soft?
        overage billed or blocked?
        what happens if the counter store is down?

means: Role-based grants permissions to named roles. Attribute-based evaluates a policy over attributes of the user, resource and context. RBAC is simple until roles explode.
example: 'Managers can approve expenses under ₹50,000 in their own department during business hours' is one ABAC policy, or a combinatorial explosion of RBAC roles.
diagram:
RBAC: user → role → permissions
  simple, auditable, roles multiply

ABAC: policy over (user, resource, action, context)
  expressive, harder to audit and debug
  "who can access X?" becomes a search problem

means: Sending reads to replicas to scale read capacity, while accepting that replicas lag. Which reads may be stale is a product decision.
example: Analytics and list views go to replicas. Anything read immediately after a write by the same user must go to the primary, or their own change appears to vanish.
diagram:
writes → primary
reads:
  ├ dashboards, lists, search → replica ✓
  └ read-after-write, balances → primary ✓

Route by query intent, not by load

means: REST is simple and cacheable. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly what they need and moves complexity server-side. gRPC is fast and typed and awkward from browsers.
example: A mobile client over-fetching 40 fields to render 6 is a GraphQL case. High-volume internal service-to-service calls are a gRPC case. A public API is usually REST.
diagram:
REST:    cacheable, simple, over/under-fetching
GraphQL: precise fetching, one endpoint,
         caching + rate limiting get hard, N+1 risk
gRPC:    binary, typed, streaming, fast
         needs a proxy for browsers

Public API → REST. Internal high-volume → gRPC.

means: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long you can afford to be down. They drive completely different investments.
example: RPO of 5 minutes means continuous WAL shipping, not nightly backups. RTO of 5 minutes means a warm standby, not a restore-from-S3 procedure.
diagram:
RPO 24h / RTO 8h  → nightly backup, manual restore
RPO 5m  / RTO 8h  → WAL shipping + manual promote
RPO 5m  / RTO 5m  → hot standby, automated failover
RPO 0   / RTO 0   → active-active, expensive

means: A central store of message schemas with enforced compatibility rules, so a producer literally cannot publish a breaking change.
example: A producer tries to remove a required field. The registry rejects the schema at publish time, instead of 40 consumers discovering it at 2am.
diagram:
producer → register schema
  registry checks compatibility (BACKWARD/FULL)
  incompatible → REJECTED at publish time ✓

Without it, the contract is tribal knowledge

means: Search is a separate system fed from your primary store, not a query against it. That means an indexing pipeline, a lag window and a reconciliation job.
example: Writing to Postgres and OpenSearch in the same request is a dual write that will drift. Feeding the index from CDC gives you a single source of truth and a measurable lag.
diagram:
Postgres (truth) → CDC → indexer → OpenSearch
                                       ↓
                                  query path

Always: measure index lag,
        run a periodic full reconcile

means: Sending a copy of real production traffic to a new system without using its responses. Real load, real data shapes, zero user risk.
example: The new search service handles a mirrored 100% of queries for two weeks. Results are diffed against the old one; nothing is served until the diff rate is near zero.
diagram:
request → old system → response to user ✓
        └→ new system → response DISCARDED
                        ↓ compare + record diffs

Watch for: duplicated side effects.
Shadow reads are safe; shadow writes are not.

means: Soft delete flags a row as deleted; hard delete removes it. Soft delete is recoverable and quietly leaks deleted data into every query that forgets the filter.
example: A `deleted_at IS NULL` filter missing from one report exposes deleted records. And soft delete is not compliant with a legal deletion request — the data is still there.
diagram:
Soft: recoverable, keeps FKs valid,
      every query must filter, table grows
Hard: gone, clean, unrecoverable

Legal erasure request → hard delete or crypto-shred.
"deleted_at" does not satisfy a deletion right.

means: Replacing a sensitive value with a meaningless reference, keeping the real value in a separate vault. It shrinks the systems in scope for compliance.
example: Storing a token instead of a card number takes your application out of PCI scope. Only the vault holds real card data, and only it needs the strictest controls.
diagram:
card 4111... → vault → token tok_9f2c

App stores the token. Vault holds the value.
Compliance scope shrinks to the vault.
Unlike encryption, the token has no math link to the value.

means: Delivering events to someone else's HTTP endpoint. You now own retries, ordering, signing and the fact that their server will be down.
example: A receiver returning 500 for six hours needs exponential retries, a dead-letter path, and signed payloads so they can verify the call really came from you.
diagram:
POST + HMAC signature + timestamp (replay window)
  → 2xx? done
  → else retry: 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 6h → disable + alert

Give receivers: an event id (dedupe),
                a replay endpoint, a delivery log

means: Changing a schema in phases so old and new code both work throughout, because during a rolling deploy both are running.
example: Renaming a column in one step breaks whichever version is mid-deploy. Expand-contract takes four releases and never breaks anything.
diagram:
1. add new column (nullable)
2. dual-write both, backfill old rows
3. switch reads to new, verify
4. stop writing old, then drop it

Four boring releases beat one exciting outage

means: The single entry point in front of your services: auth, rate limiting, routing, request shaping.
example: Mobile clients hit one gateway. It validates the JWT once, applies per-key rate limits, and routes to six internal services that no longer need their own auth code.
diagram:
Client → Gateway
          ├ authn/authz
          ├ rate limit
          ├ route
          └ aggregate
       → internal services

means: A dedicated gateway per client type, so a mobile app isn't forced to consume an API shaped for a web dashboard.
example: Web needs 40 fields; mobile needs 6 and is on a slow connection. One shared endpoint over-fetches for mobile. Two BFFs let each shape its own payload.
diagram:
Web app    → Web BFF    → services
Mobile app → Mobile BFF → services

Each BFF owns its own aggregation shape

means: During a network partition, you choose consistency or availability. You never get to skip the partition — networks fail.
example: Two data centres lose their link. A CP system rejects writes on the minority side to stay correct. An AP system accepts them and reconciles later, risking conflicts.
diagram:
Partition happens (not optional)
   ↓
CP → reject writes, stay correct
AP → accept writes, reconcile later

'CA' is not a real production choice

means: Streaming a database's write-ahead log as events, so downstream systems learn about changes without polling or dual writes.
example: Debezium tails the Postgres WAL and publishes every row change to Kafka. Search index, cache and analytics warehouse all update from one source of truth.
diagram:
Postgres WAL
   ↓ Debezium
Kafka topic (row changes)
   ├→ search index
   ├→ cache invalidation
   └→ analytics warehouse

means: Different machines disagree about the current time. Any logic that compares timestamps across servers is quietly wrong.
example: Two nodes' clocks differ by 400ms. 'Last write wins' by timestamp silently discards the newer write. Use logical clocks or a single sequencer instead.
diagram:
Node A clock: 12:00:00.000
Node B clock: 11:59:59.600
   ↓
last-write-wins picks the wrong one
Fix: logical clocks, version vectors, DB sequence

means: Mapping keys to nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node only remaps 1/N of keys, not all of them.
example: With `hash % N`, going from 8 to 9 cache nodes invalidates ~89% of keys at once. With consistent hashing, only ~11% move.
diagram:
0°
       node A ●
            ╱   ╲
   key k → ●     ● node B
           │     │
   node D  ●     ● node C
            ╲   ╱
              ●
each key walks clockwise to the next node

add node E → only keys between D and E move
hash % N   → 8→9 nodes remaps 89% ✗
the ring   → 8→9 nodes remaps 11% ✓

means: Separating the write model from the read model so each can be shaped for its own job.
example: Writes go to a normalised Postgres schema. Reads come from a denormalised Elasticsearch projection built from the write stream. Read latency drops; you now own the sync lag.
diagram:
Command → write model (normalised)
              ↓ events
Query   ← read model (denormalised)

Faster reads, eventual consistency between them

means: A lock held in shared storage so only one process across the fleet does something. Correct only with a TTL and a fencing token.
example: A Redis lock with SET NX PX 30000 prevents two workers from processing the same file. Without a TTL, a crashed holder blocks the job forever.
diagram:
SET lock:job1 <uuid> NX PX 30000
  acquired? → do work → DEL if uuid matches
  no?       → skip

No TTL = deadlock on crash
No token = zombie writes

means: Storing the sequence of changes as the source of truth, and deriving current state by replaying them. Powerful, and heavier than teams expect.
example: Instead of an `balance = 400` row, you store Deposited 500, Withdrew 100. You get a perfect audit log and time travel — and every schema change becomes a replay problem.
diagram:
Events (immutable, append-only)
  Deposited 500
  Withdrew  100
     ↓ fold
  State: balance 400

Rebuild any past state by replaying

means: Replicas converge to the same value if writes stop. Between write and convergence, different readers can see different truths.
example: User updates their avatar. Replica in Mumbai shows the new one instantly; the read replica in Frankfurt shows the old one for 300ms. Fine for avatars, not for account balances.
diagram:
t=0    write to primary
t=0ms  replica A: new ✓
t=300  replica B: old  ← stale read window
t=310  replica B: new ✓ converged

means: Precompute results for every consumer at write time, or compute per request at read time. The classic timeline problem.
example: A celebrity with 50M followers posts. Fan-out on write means 50M inserts for one action. Fan-out on read means 50M timeline queries. Real systems do both, split by follower count.
diagram:
Write fan-out: 1 post → 50M feed rows
  fast reads, brutal celebrity writes
Read fan-out: query followed authors at load
  cheap writes, slow reads
Hybrid: normal users write, celebs read

means: A monotonically increasing number handed out with a lock, so a resumed zombie process can be rejected as stale.
example: Node A holds a lock, GC-pauses for 20s, loses the lease. Node B takes it with token 34. Node A wakes and writes with token 33 — storage rejects it.
diagram:
A acquires lock → token 33
A pauses (GC)
B acquires lock → token 34 → writes ✓
A wakes, writes token 33 → REJECTED ✓

means: One shard receiving disproportionate traffic because the partition key isn't uniformly distributed.
example: Sharding events by `tenant_id` looks fine until one enterprise customer produces 60% of all events. That shard saturates while the other 15 idle.
diagram:
shard 0  ████████████████ 60% (BigCorp)
shard 1  ██
shard 2  █
   ↓
Fix: composite key tenant_id + bucket

means: Picking exactly one node to coordinate, and detecting fast when it dies. Every 'only one worker should do this' problem is this problem.
example: Three schedulers run; without election all three fire the same cron. With a lease in Redis or etcd, only the lease holder runs and the others stand by.
diagram:
3 schedulers, 1 lease key
  A holds lease → runs cron
  B, C          → standby
A dies → lease expires (10s) → B takes over

means: Writing your domain change and the event to publish in the same DB transaction, then relaying the event separately. Removes the dual-write bug.
example: Naively: save the order, then publish to RabbitMQ. The broker call fails and the order exists with no event. With an outbox both writes commit atomically and a relay drains the table.
diagram:
BEGIN
  INSERT order
  INSERT outbox(event)
COMMIT              ← atomic
   ↓
relay polls outbox → publish → mark sent

means: Requiring a majority for reads and writes so the two sets always overlap by at least one node holding the latest value.
example: N=3 replicas, W=2, R=2. Any read touches at least one node that saw the last write. Setting W=1, R=1 is fast and returns stale data.
diagram:
N=5   [1][2][3][4][5]
W=3   [1][2][3]
R=3         [3][4][5]
             ↑ overlap guaranteed

R + W >  N  → 3+3 > 5 ✓ read sees the last write
R + W <= N  → 2+2 < 5 ✗ read can miss it

W up → durability.  R up → freshness.

means: The weakest guarantee users actually notice: after I write something, I must see it. Someone else seeing it late is fine.
example: User edits a comment, is routed to a read replica, and their own edit vanishes. Fix: pin that user's session to the primary for a few seconds after writing.
diagram:
Write → primary
Read  → replica (lagging) → old value ✗

Fix: sticky read-from-primary window
     or pass a write timestamp/LSN

means: How far behind a replica is from the primary, measured in time or bytes. It's zero in the design doc and never zero in production.
example: A batch job writes 2M rows. Replica lag climbs to 45 seconds. Every read-replica query for the next minute returns stale data, and dashboards show 'missing' orders.
diagram:
Primary  LSN 9,000,412
Replica  LSN 8,997,001
   ↓
lag = 45 sec

Alert on lag, not just on replica 'up'

means: Replacing a distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it.
example: Book flight → charge card → reserve hotel. Hotel fails, so you run 'refund card' then 'cancel flight'. There's no rollback, only compensation.
diagram:
T1 flight ✓ → T2 charge ✓ → T3 hotel ✗
              ↓ compensate backwards
C2 refund ✓ ← C1 cancel flight ✓

Eventually consistent, never atomic

means: How a service finds the current network address of another, when instances come and go constantly.
example: Hardcoded IPs break the moment autoscaling replaces a pod. Kubernetes DNS resolves `payments.prod.svc` to whatever healthy pods exist right now.
diagram:
Instance starts → registers (or gets Endpoint)
Caller asks registry/DNS → healthy addresses
Instance dies → deregistered

Hardcoded IPs = guaranteed 3am page

means: The control plane that configures all those sidecars centrally: traffic policy, mTLS, retries and observability across every service.
example: Istio lets you shift 10% of traffic to v2 and enforce mTLS everywhere from one config, instead of changing 40 codebases.
diagram:
Control plane (policy, certs, routing)
   ↓ configures
[sidecar][sidecar][sidecar]
   ↓
Uniform retries, mTLS, traffic splits
Cost: real operational complexity

means: Splitting data horizontally across independent databases by a key, so no single node holds everything.
example: Users are sharded by `hash(user_id) % 16`. Each shard holds ~6% of the data. Cross-shard queries — 'all orders last month' — become genuinely hard.
diagram:
hash(user_id) % 16 → shard
  shard 0  users A, D, K...
  shard 15 users B, F, Z...

Easy: single-user reads
Hard: joins, global aggregates, resharding

means: Running a helper container alongside your app in the same pod to handle cross-cutting concerns like mTLS, retries and telemetry.
example: Envoy sits next to every service. Your Node app makes a plain HTTP call; the sidecar adds mutual TLS, retries and tracing headers without a line of app code.
diagram:
┌──────── Pod ────────┐
│  app  ↔  sidecar    │ → network
│           (Envoy)   │
└─────────────────────┘
mTLS, retries, tracing — outside your code

means: A partition leaves two nodes each believing they are the primary. Both accept writes; the data diverges irreconcilably.
example: Network blips between two DB nodes. Both promote themselves. For 40 seconds each takes writes. Merging afterwards means picking which customer's orders to discard.
diagram:
✂ partition
Node A "I'm primary" ← writes
Node B "I'm primary" ← writes
   ↓
divergent history, manual repair
Fix: quorum-based election / fencing

means: Replacing a legacy system incrementally by routing individual endpoints to new code until nothing is left of the old one.
example: The proxy sends /orders to the new service and everything else to the monolith. Over eight months routes migrate one by one. There is never a big-bang cutover.
diagram:
Proxy
   ┌────┴────┐
new service  legacy monolith
 /orders     /everything-else
   ↓ month by month
new service  (monolith shrinks to nothing)

means: Every read returns the most recent committed write, always. You pay for it in latency and availability.
example: A ledger balance must be strongly consistent — reading a stale balance lets a user double-spend. That means reads go to the primary or through a quorum.
diagram:
write → commit → visible everywhere
   ↓
reads must coordinate (quorum / primary)
   ↓
higher latency, lower availability
Worth it for money, not for like counts
